title: Where distros differ
summary: Init systems, filesystems, admin groups, firewalls and mandatory access control, and sudo drop-ins done safely.

steps.title: Init: systemd and OpenRC
body: Almost every mainstream distro uses **systemd** (module 4). The notable exception is **Alpine**, which uses **OpenRC** (also Gentoo, Artix), and minimal containers often run no init at all.
| start / stop / restart | `systemctl start nginx` | `rc-service nginx start` |
| start at boot | `systemctl enable nginx` | `rc-update add nginx default` |
| don't start at boot | `systemctl disable nginx` | `rc-update del nginx default` |

steps.prompt: Match the systemd command to its OpenRC twin.

steps.title: Filesystems, admin groups, firewalls, MAC
body: **Default filesystems**: Debian/Ubuntu **ext4**; RHEL/Rocky/Alma **xfs** (cannot shrink); Fedora Workstation and openSUSE **btrfs** (snapshots, compression, subvolumes; openSUSE rolls back bad updates with snapper).
**Admin group**: members may use sudo. Debian/Ubuntu: `sudo` group (`usermod -aG sudo ana`). RHEL/Fedora/Arch/SUSE: `wheel` (`usermod -aG wheel ana`). Check `/etc/sudoers` for `%sudo` or `%wheel`.

**Firewall front-ends** (both drive nftables underneath): Ubuntu **ufw** (`ufw allow 443/tcp`, `ufw enable`); RHEL/Fedora/SUSE **firewalld** with zones (`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https`, then `--reload`).

**Mandatory access control** (rules that even root processes must obey): RHEL/Fedora **SELinux** labels every file and process (`ls -Z`, `getenforce`, `restorecon`, `setsebool`); Ubuntu/Debian/SUSE **AppArmor** uses per-program path profiles (`aa-status`, profiles in `/etc/apparmor.d`). When a service "has permission" but still gets `Permission denied` on RHEL, check `ausearch -m avc` before anything else, and never "fix" it with `setenforce 0`.

steps.prompt: On Rocky Linux, nginx gets `Permission denied` reading `/srv/site/index.html`, even though the file is `644` and the directories are `755`. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: SELinux: the files lack the `httpd_sys_content_t` label; fix it with `semanage fcontext` + `restorecon`, not by disabling SELinux
nginx needs to run as root
steps.explain: Files created outside the standard web root get a default label that the web server's SELinux domain may not read.

steps.title: sudo rights, the safe way
prompt: Admin rights differ by family: Debian and Ubuntu give them to the group **`sudo`**, RHEL, Fedora and Arch to **`wheel`**.
This machine is Debian. Use `getent group sudo wheel` to see what exists.
1. Make `ana` a full admin the Debian way: add her to the right group.
2. Let `deploy` run **only** `/usr/bin/systemctl restart shop` as root, without a password, through a drop-in file
3. A teammate wrote `~/staging/90-ops` for the `ops` group. **Validate it before installing it**: one broken file in
`/etc/sudoers.d` breaks `sudo` for everyone. Fix it and install it as `/etc/sudoers.d/90-ops` (mode `440`).
`visudo -cf FILE` checks a file without installing it. `sudo -l -U USER` shows what a user may run.

checks.name: ana is in the sudo group
checks.fail: `ana` is not in the `sudo` group: `sudo usermod -aG sudo ana`.

checks.name: the whole sudoers configuration is valid
checks.fail: `sudo visudo -c` reports an error (below). Fix the file it names.

checks.name: deploy may restart shop, and nothing else
checks.cmd: l=$(sudo -l -U deploy 2>/dev/null); echo "$l" | grep -q "NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart shop" && ! echo "$l" | grep -Eq "\(ALL( : ALL)?\) (NOPASSWD: )?ALL$"
checks.fail: `sudo -l -U deploy` should list exactly `(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart shop`.

checks.name: the ops team has its rights
checks.fail: `sudo -l -U omar` (he is in `ops`) should show `NOPASSWD: ALL`. Is `/etc/sudoers.d/90-ops` installed and fixed?

checks.name: both drop-ins are mode 440
checks.fail: Both files in `/etc/sudoers.d` should be `440` (sudo ignores files others can write). `sudo install -m 440 SRC DEST` copies with the mode in one go.

hints: `sudo usermod -aG sudo ana`. On Rocky it would be `wheel`.

Write and validate in your home first: `echo 'deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart shop' > ~/deploy.sudo && visudo -cf ~/deploy.sudo`, then `sudo install -m 440 ~/deploy.sudo /etc/sudoers.d/deploy`.
`visudo -cf ~/staging/90-ops` points at the typo in `NOPASWD`. Fix it with `sed -i`, check again, then `sudo install -m 440 ~/staging/90-ops /etc/sudoers.d/90-ops`.
explain: Drop-in files in `/etc/sudoers.d` are how configuration tools manage sudo: one file per role, easy to add and remove.
Always validate first (`visudo -cf`, or edit with `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/x`, which refuses to save a broken
file): a syntax error locks every admin out of `sudo` until someone gets a root shell another way. Rights limited to
one command are what CI deploy users should get, never `ALL`.
